q: The regex has already checked that the method is one of the four allowed words. Why does `method: m[2]` still not compile as a `Method`?
options: Regex captures are typed `string`. The compiler can't read the pattern, so you assert with `as Method` after the regex has checked it
`m[2]` is the whole match, not the second group
explain: TypeScript doesn't analyse regular expressions, so every capture is just `string`. Here the regex really does guarantee one of the four words, so `m[2] as Method` is a safe, justified assertion. Types don't exist at runtime, and `m[0]` (not `m[2]`) is the whole match.

q: Which containers are a good fit for these jobs? Select all that apply.
options: `Record<"2xx" | "3xx" | "4xx" | "5xx", number>` for counts per status class
`[path: string, ms: number] | null` for the slowest request
`any` for the report, so it's flexible
explain: A `Record` over the literal union guarantees all four buckets exist. A `Set` dedupes for free, and its `.size` is the count. A tuple-or-`null` says "two values, or nothing" exactly. A `string[]` with `includes` works, but it gets slower as it grows and you have to remember to check before every push. `any` throws away all the checking you'd want in a tool people rely on at 2 a.m.

`split` cuts at **every** `\n`: the first request, an empty string (the blank line), the second request, and a final empty string after the trailing newline. That's 4. That's why the analyser trims each line and treats empty ones as blank, rather than counting them as unreadable.
